'Will hand keys to UN': Trump-appointed Board of Peace adviser says Israel blocking efforts
items.content:
'Will hand keys to UN': Trump-appointed Board of Peace adviser says Israel blocking efforts
Submitted by
Daniel Tester
on
Sat, 11/21/2026 - 13:27
The board said it was frustrated by Israel's obstructions while Gaza remains trapped in a deepening humanitarian crisis
Palestinians walk past destroyed buildings and displacement tents in Khan Younis, southern Gaza Strip, 17 November 2026 (Eyad Baba/AFP)
Off
A senior adviser to the
US
-led Board of Peace for Gaza has said that the panel “will hand the keys” to the enclave to the UN if Israel continues to block efforts to prepare for an international stabilisation force and disarm Hamas.
“We have been extremely patient and have given Israel its space,” US official Josh Gruenbaum told the
Israeli
news site Ynet in an interview published on Friday.
But he said that it was “frustrating” that “Israel is failing to move forward on the commitments Prime Minister Netanyahu made to President Trump”.
Chaired by US President Donald Trump, the Board of Peace was
given
a sweeping mandate by the UN Security Council in November 2025 to establish an international stabilisation force in Gaza as part of a
20-point plan
to end hostilities and rehabilitate the devastated enclave.
While the plan features several Israeli demands, including the full demilitarisation of the Gaza Strip, talks have stalled for months amid
disputes
over Hamas’ weapons handover and ongoing Israeli attacks, which have killed over 1,600
Palestinians
in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire.
Hamas formally
accepted
the Board of Peace’s roadmap in July, agreeing to hand over its weapons to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a technocratic Palestinian body inaugurated and overseen by the US-led board.
But since then, Israel has continually refused to sign an agreement that would permit the stabilisation forces to deploy, and has blocked vetted members of Gaza’s police force from leaving the enclave to undertake training ahead of the planned weapons handover.
Israel has also refused to allow the construction of military outposts that would serve as barracks for the stabilisation force's troops, according to reports in
the Guardian.
Full text: 15-point draft peace plan between Hamas and Israel in Gaza
Read More »
“We are at a standstill due to political elements within the Netanyahu government, who have prevented us from progressing and from testing whether Hamas will keep its word,” Gruenbaum added.
Gruenbaum, a Jewish-American former private equity investor who also serves as a commissioner for the US government’s Federal Acquisition Service, was appointed by Trump in January to manage the day-to-day operations of the board, alongside the controversial diplomatic adviser
Aryeh Lightstone
.
Israel has killed over 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza since the Hamas attacks of October 2023 as the enclave faces an ongoing catastrophic humanitarian crisis, with 65 percent of its residents - around 1.4 million people - living in makeshift shelters or tents.
Many of these shelters were destroyed amid flooding earlier this month, which rights monitors called an “utterly preventable tragedy” fuelled by Israel’s ongoing blockade of the aid and supplies needed to repair vital infrastructure.
“A catastrophic winter is approaching for Gaza. We have already seen numerous headlines about flooding," Gruenbaum added in the Ynet interview.
"Israel needs to heed the international community’s call to avert this crisis."

items.title: SNL’s skit Sister captures the quiet agony of caregiving for women: ‘I’ve never felt seen like that’
items.content:
The viral satirization of the caregiving burden left to women and daughters hit home for many viewers
The
Saturday Night Live
sketch
, titled Sister quickly went viral this week for its satirization of the burden that women and daughters face to take care of aging family members. In the parody commercial, comedian John Mulaney touts the benefit of “Sister”, who he describes as “a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister” .
“Now I don’t have to worry about dad getting the care and attention he needs because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life, and the stuff I like to do,” Mulaney says, as the sister, played by cast member Jane Wickline, gives their father’s medication to him.
The sketch, which amassed over seven million views on YouTube in less than a week since it aired, has received thousands of responses and comments about its accuracy.
“This is one of the MOST wicked and spot on SNL sketches ever written,” wrote one commenter on YouTube. Another posted: “As a hospice nurse this definitely tracks. I deal 90% of the time with adult daughters, and if there is no daughter, it is the daughter in law.”
“This is so real it almost gave me a stroke from rage,” added another viewer.

items.title: Federal judge denies request to release man shot by immigration agents in New York
items.content:
Oscar Belgal, a Dominican national, was shot by ICE agents as he drove his five-year-old son home from school
A federal judge on Friday declined to release from custody a man who was
shot and wounded
by immigration officers as they arrested him in
New York
in October.
The US district court judge Hector Gonzalez said in a written ruling that agents may have made a procedural error in serving an arrest warrant on Oscar Belgal before he was given a notice to appear in immigration court. However, he wrote, that was merely a technical error that does not require Belgal to be released from federal custody pending deportation proceedings.

items.title: COP31 climate summit risks failure as talks go deep into overtime
items.content:
By Valerie Volcovici and Sarah McFarlane
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 21 (Reuters) - The COP31 climate summit will either produce a good deal or no deal at all, the European Union's top climate official said on Saturday as talks stretched deep into overtime.
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are struggling to bridge divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance, delaying an agreement at the two-week conference that had been scheduled to end on Friday.

items.title: ‘Hell dorm’: Florida prisoners testify about 119F heat indexes and walls that sweat
items.content:
Temperatures in a concrete facility contributed to one man’s death after he struggled to breathe, prisoners allege
On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami,
Florida
, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”
Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the
Florida Justice Institute
, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that
Stefano Shiavon
, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,” Wilson said. “It’s miserable in the cell at night because, again, it’s so hot. No air comes to the bed we sleep at and the bed is soaked in sweat.”

items.content:
الدانمارك تدعو الاتحاد الأوروبي لتشديد قيود السفرعلى الروس بعد محاولة اغتيال مغني راب أمريكي
دعت الدانمارك، الجمعة، دول الاتحاد الأوروبي إلى اتخاذ خطوات ملموسة للتصدي لروسيا، مقترحة فرض قيود إضافية على دخول المواطنين الروس إلى منطقة "شنغن"، وذلك في أعقاب إعلان كوبنهاغن إحباط محاولة اغتيال استهدفت مغني راب أمريكي أوكراني على أراضيها، قالت إنها من تدبير أجهزة الاستخبارات الروسية وأعلنت على خلفيتها طرد الملحق العسكري الروسي. من جهتها قالت السفارة ​الروسية في كوبنهاغن إن الاتهامات لا تستند إلى أدلة.

items.title: Iran claims to have struck US F-16 jet
items.content:
Iran claims to have struck US F-16 jet
Iran
's army has claimed that its air defence systems struck a
US
F-16 fighter jet with a missile on Friday evening, damaging the aircraft.
Iranian state media reported that the strike forced the plane to divert course and make an emergency landing.
The US military, which has seen few casualties throughout the war, has not commented on the incident.
This is a developing story. We'll bring you more updates when we get them.

items.title: الله اكبر
items.content:
الله اكبر

مشاهد من استهداف طائرة اف 16 الامريكية يوم امس في الاجواء الايرانية

الجيش الايراني: في مساء يوم الجمعة، تمكنت أنظمة الدفاع الجوي المحلية التابعة للجيش، المنتشرة في جنوب البلاد، والتي تخضع لسيطرة الشبكة الموحدة للدفاع الجوي في البلاد، من تحديد موقع طائرة مقاتلة من طراز F-16 أمريكية فوق الخليج العربي.

خلال هذه العملية، وبعد اعتراض الطائرة الأمريكية من طراز F16، قامت الأنظمة الدفاعية بإطلاق صاروخ باتجاهها. ونتيجة لانفجار الصاروخ بالقرب من الطائرة، تعرضت الطائرة الأمريكية المهاجمة لأضرار، واضطر طيارها إلى إلغاء المهمة والهبوط الاضطراري في أحد أقرب المطارات في المنطقة.

items.title: US pursuit of ‘Trump-class’ warships has blown cost of new fleet by billions, report warns
items.content:
Iran war stretching fleet’s capacity, navy chief admits, as CBO finds estimated cost of new ships ‘unrealistically low’
The US navy’s commitment to the new Trump-class battleships has blown out the cost of its new fleet by billions of dollars, a report to the US Congress has found, as the acting secretary of the navy conceded this week the Iran war was “stretching” the fleet’s capacity.
The challenges facing the world’s biggest naval force were highlighted this week, when the return of the USS George Washington from the Middle East on Wednesday ended a rare three-month period when the US had no aircraft carrier across all of the Pacific. Deployments have been regularly running beyond 300 days, with the maintenance and repair of ships deferred so they can stay at sea longer.

items.title: ‘Music was our teacher’: the sound system pioneers reviving the scene in Manchester and beyond
items.content:
Manchester-based Megatone Sound Foundation and Baron Turbo Charge have rejuvenated the culture to offer a sense of belonging and empowerment
For a generation of young Black Mancunians, some of the history lessons that mattered most were not taught in classrooms, but through towering stacks of amps and speakers, turntables and Jamaican records.
“We didn’t know where we fit in. We didn’t know our history. Our parents were busy working two or three jobs,” says Errol “Barzy” Beaumont, a founder member of Baron Turbo Charge, Manchester’s long-running reggae sound system. “It was the records – Burning Spear, Bob Marley,
Culture,
that were telling us about our culture, which wasn’t on the school curriculum. For us, the sound system was not just entertainment – it was an education.”

items.title: Iran says new air defence system intercepted US Reaper drone over Hormuz
items.content:
Iran says new air defence system intercepted US Reaper drone over Hormuz
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Sat, 11/21/2026 - 09:50
The US reported losing at least 45 Reaper drones by August, while Iran says its forces have now destroyed 58 since the war began
A crew member monitors an MQ-9 Reaper military drone at Cognac air base in Chateaubernard, southwestern France, 12 June 2026 (Christophe Archambault/AFP)
Off
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it shot down a
US
MQ-9 Reaper drone in the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported on Saturday.
The IRGC
said
it is the 58th aircraft destroyed by
Iranian
forces since the start of the war, adding that the drone was detected, tracked and destroyed by Iran’s new air defence system.
In August, the US military
said
that it had lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during the war, amounting to roughly a quarter of its fleet, according to three US officials cited by The Washington Post.
The newspaper estimated the losses could represent more than $1.3bn in equipment costs.
The development comes amid renewed tensions between Washington and Tehran, with attacks on commercial vessels near the Strait of Hormuz.
A commercial tanker was hit by an unknown missile about 11 nautical miles north of Khasab port in Oman, in the Strait of Hormuz, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO)
said
.
The US military
said
on Tuesday that it had
attacked a missile launching site
on Iran’s Qeshm Island in retaliation for attacks by Iran on US personnel and property.
Iran later
said
it had attacked US drone and missile facilities at the Ali al-Salem air base in Kuwait.
US builds up forces around Iran, but can it sustain another war?
Read More »
Kuwait reported responding to "hostile drone activity", while Bahrain said it had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks.
The conflict, launched by the US and Israel on 28 February, has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The strait is one of the world's most important energy corridors. In 2025, around 25 per cent of world oil trade by sea was
carried
through the Strait of Hormuz.
A memorandum of understanding was signed in June between the two nations
to continue dialogue
about issues such as free passage within the strait, Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities and sanctions.
The agreement did not produce a lasting settlement, and the parties have continued to disagree over maritime security and the terms of a broader deal.
Blockade and negotiations
Washington has stepped up economic pressure on Tehran as the two sides remain at odds over the conditions for ending the war and restoring navigation through the strait.
The US Treasury has
imposed sanctions
against four people for acting as "oil trustees" and facilitating the movement of revenues from international sales of Iranian oil in order to help Tehran avoid sanctions and the US-imposed blockade.
Mossad abducted Iranian general in Turkey, tortured him for weeks before killing him: Report
Read More »
Those hit by the sanctions include the former intelligence officer of the IRGC, Mohammad Javad Bavand, and Majid Taj, brother of the president of the Iranian Football Federation, Mehdi Taj.
Under these sanctions, all assets held by the individuals in the US are frozen. Additionally, none of these individuals can conduct business with individuals or companies based in the US, unless in compliance with relevant regulations and authorisations.
The blockades began on 13 April. US Central Command has
said
it will block sea traffic to and from Iranian ports and waters. However, ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz to and from ports outside Iran will be allowed to pass unhindered.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi
said
on Friday that the blockade must be broken to allow the country to resume oil exports.
“We are making every possible effort regarding oil exports and negotiations. The naval blockade must be broken,” he told reporters in Tehran.
Araghchi has also said Iran’s seven conditions must be met before the Strait of Hormuz can reopen. The demands include an end to the war and the lifting of sanctions and the US blockade, according to his recent statements.
He said Tehran was prepared to discuss how the conditions could be implemented, but that negotiations depended on Washington taking confidence-building measures.

items.title: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears
items.content:
Experts say BBLs and other cosmetic procedures can be risky and seasonal offers at clinics in England could make people rush decisions
Clinics in England are promoting seasonal deals – including for Black Friday – on liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), despite concerns about the risks of the procedure.
The
government is consulting on limiting liquid BBLs
, vampire facials and deep chemical peels in England to qualified healthcare professionals. The proposals follow the death of Alice Webb, a 33-year-old mother of five, after a botched liquid BBL in a Gloucester salon in 2024. Her family have
called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys”
to be introduced before more people die.

items.title: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
items.content:
Foreign combatants in Port-au-Prince welcomed by many after years of gang control but some fear offensive could exacerbate volatile situation
A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker Emmanuel Sanon covers the facade of Port-au-Prince’s main football ground. But more than two years have passed since any sports stars graced the pitch.
In 2024, as the surrounding city was
almost entirely captured by heavily armed gangs
, Sylvio Cator stadium – where football greats including Brazil’s Ronaldo and Roberto Carlos once played – also fell under criminal control, its dilapidated red and blue stands used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss called Izo. Haiti’s national team, the Grenadiers, found itself homeless and was
forced to play its World Cup qualifying games abroad
.

items.title: Explosive-laden boxes dropped from the sky: Israel’s latest weapon in Gaza
items.content:
Explosive-laden boxes dropped from the sky: Israel’s latest weapon in Gaza
Jaber Yaseen's family was preparing the traditional maftoul dish for their Friday family lunch when they heard a loud engine approaching.
The Palestinian family of 13 were startled by the noise, which grew louder as it approached their home in the al-Zaytoon neighbourhood, east of Gaza City.
“I thought it was an Israeli tank at first. I looked out of the window and was shocked to see a huge quadcopter drone carrying two boxes of explosives, flying low over our neighbourhood,” Yaseen told Middle East Eye.
“I watched the drone move towards us. Without any warning, it dropped the two boxes of explosives onto our roof. I was terrified for my children's lives. I grabbed them and rushed out of the house, knowing the explosives could detonate at any moment. We couldn't take anything with us.”

items.title: Explosive-laden boxes dropped from the sky: Israel’s latest weapon in Gaza
items.content:
Explosive-laden boxes dropped from the sky: Israel’s latest weapon in Gaza
Submitted by
Abdallah al-Naami
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 12:08
Palestinian families recount how Israeli quadcopters drop explosives on to their homes, demolishing entire buildings and displacing dozens of families
Jaber Yaseen stands amid the rubble of his home, destroyed by explosive-laden boxes dropped by an Israeli drone in Gaza City’s al-Zaytoon neighbourhood (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
Off
Jaber Yaseen's family was preparing the traditional maftoul dish for their Friday family lunch when they heard a loud engine approaching.
The
Palestinian
family of 13 were startled by the noise, which grew louder as it approached their home in al-Zaytoon neighbourhood, east of Gaza City.
“I thought it was an Israeli tank at first. I looked out of the window and was shocked to see a huge quadcopter drone carrying two boxes of explosives, flying low over our neighbourhood,” Yaseen told Middle East Eye.
“I watched the drone move towards us. Without any warning, it dropped the two boxes of explosives on to our roof. I was terrified for my children's lives. I grabbed them and rushed out of the house, knowing the explosives could detonate at any moment. We couldn't take anything with us.”
Panic spread as families watched more
Israeli
drones dropping explosives on to rooftops across the neighbourhood. Dozens were forced to flee their homes, with nowhere to go.
A group of residents gathered at a distance, watching as the quadcopter drones continued to drop explosives. Minutes later, the devices on the rooftops began detonating.
For 33-year-old Ismail Madi, watching the drones was heartbreaking.
“We had been displaced several times before, and each time I held on to some hope that we would return home. But when I saw the quadcopter drones carrying explosives above our home, I felt as though I had left my soul behind as I walked away,” Madi told MEE.
Abdaljawad Badwan, another resident of the neighbourhood, described the terror of watching the attack unfold.
“Everyone was shocked and terrified. Every time an explosion went off, we hoped it would be the last. But the drones kept coming back with more boxes.”
Three multi-storey houses were destroyed in the attack on 13 November 2026 (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
Families told MEE that the initial explosions were intended to create openings in the roofs.
Large quadcopter drones, measuring approximately 4m across, then continued to drop nearly 60 boxes of explosives inside each house.
The explosives were subsequently detonated, destroying the houses and damaging many surrounding buildings.
By 10pm (8pm GMT), the Israeli attack on 13 November had completely demolished three multi-storey houses and severely damaged dozens of others.
Nearly 33 families lost their homes that night.
Forced into the streets
With their homes destroyed, Palestinian families were left without shelter in the cold night.
“We had nowhere to go for shelter. All 13 of us spent the night on the pavement. We are still living on the pavement in a makeshift tent that I built the following day,” Yaseen said.
The sudden displacement has compounded the suffering these families were already enduring.
“We spent the night on the street, surrounded by piles of rubbish, rodents and insects. My two-year-old son, Abdalsamad, was very sick, and I had to go around asking neighbours for painkillers late at night,” said Badwan, a father of four.
'I built this home brick by brick. I don't know how to describe what I feel'
-
Jaber Yaseen, Gaza resident
In the early hours of the morning, families returned to inspect their homes. They were confronted with scenes of devastation.
“I have lived here my entire life, yet I could barely recognise my neighbourhood because of the sheer scale of destruction,” Madi said.
For him, the aftermath was particularly devastating. He had married just two months earlier.
“I put a lifetime of hard work into preparing my home and saving for my wedding. I had hoped to begin a new chapter of my life there, with a sense of stability and safety. I was overwhelmed with grief when I saw my home and everything I had worked for destroyed before my eyes,” Madi told MEE.
Standing amid the rubble of his home, Yaseen struggled to put his feelings into words.
“I built this home brick by brick. I don't know how to describe what I feel. It's heartbreaking. I find myself crying every night just thinking about my home,” he told MEE.
‘We face death every day’
Since returning to their neighbourhood following the October 2025 ceasefire agreement, families in al-Zaytoon have faced a daily struggle for survival.
Being located near the so-called "Yellow Line" - a military boundary imposed by Israeli forces inside the Gaza Strip - has meant a consistent threat from Israeli soldiers nearby.
“We face death every day,” Madi told MEE.
“The Yellow Line is just 50m away. Israeli quadcopter drones and tanks come every day and open fire towards our homes. These attacks have become part of our daily routine. We have no choice but to adapt. We have even taught the children how to hide when the shooting starts.”
Israel’s expanding ‘Yellow Line’ swallows Gaza districts and uproots families
Read More »
Israeli forces have steadily pushed the "Yellow Line" westwards over the past year, encroaching on residential areas, often without warning.
“We have lived in constant danger for the past year. We could wake up any day to find that the [Israeli] army has moved the yellow blocks westwards, past our homes, and that we have to evacuate,” Yaseen said.
The daily attacks are not the only hardship these families face. Living in an area classified as dangerous by humanitarian aid organisations, they receive little to no assistance.
Families say that the nearest source of water, medical centre or school is 2km away. Adults and children must make the dangerous journey every day, despite the recurring Israeli attacks.
“We have adapted to the daily Israeli attacks and the lack of aid because we wanted to stay in our homes. The quadcopter attack was shocking. I never imagined something like this could happen, especially without any warning,” Yaseen said.
A new tactic to displace families?
Despite the so-called ceasefire in Gaza, Israel has continued its attacks in Gaza, killing at least 1,600 Palestinians, destroying homes and expanding its control through military force.
Last week's attack on al-Zaytoon neighbourhood marked a new development, with Israeli forces using quadcopter drones to plant boxes of explosives inside homes in a populated area outside the "Yellow Line". Families had barely enough time to escape before watching their homes being destroyed.
The attack was not an isolated incident.
'I was born and raised in this home. I cannot live away from it'
- Ismail Madi, Gaza resident
Over the past week, Israel has escalated its use of quadcopter drones carrying boxes of explosives, destroying Palestinian homes and property outside the "Yellow Line" in al-Maghazi, al-Musadder, Khan Younis and al-Nuseirat.
As these attacks grow in intensity and frequency, families across Gaza fear that explosive-laden quadcopter drones are becoming a central part of Israel's tactics to destroy what remains of Palestinian homes in Gaza and forcibly displace residents.
“We are worried that Friday's attack was a message or a threat from the [Israeli] army telling us to leave the area, and that perhaps we won't be allowed to return to it in the near future,” Yaseen told MEE.
On Thursday, for the first time since the so-called ceasefire, Israel announced the launch of a ground attack outside the "Yellow Line" in al-Nuseirat, in central Gaza.
During the preceding night, Israeli forces destroyed several buildings in northern al-Nuseirat using boxes of explosives planted by quadcopter drones.
Despite the destruction, Ismail Madi returns to his home, which he sees as the community’s first line of defence (Abdallah al-Naami/MEE)
But despite the destruction of their homes and the catastrophic conditions they face, families were quick to return to al-Zaytoon neighbourhood after the attack.
“I spend the day here in the neighbourhood. My soul is attached to my home, even though it is now just a pile of rubble,” Yaseen told MEE.
“I'll build my tent here, next to the remains of my home. I'd rather die than live away from home.”
For Madi, returning to the neighbourhood is about more than his attachment to his home.
“I was born and raised in this home. I cannot live away from it,” he told MEE.
“By staying here in the neighbourhood, we are the first line of defence for the community. Our steadfastness gives other families living near the Yellow Line a sense of hope and safety.”

items.title: UK, France and China vote against UAE's Lana Nusseibeh at UN
items.content:
UK, France and China vote against UAE's Lana Nusseibeh at UN
Lana Nusseibeh's bid to become the next secretary-general of the United Nations suffered a setback on Friday after the
UK
,
France
and
China
all voted against the Emirati diplomat in the latest informal straw poll conducted to help determine who should replace Antonio Guterres.
Along with the
US
and
Russia
, the countries make up three of the P5, the permanent members of the UN Security Council that can veto any prospective candidate for the world body's top job.
While votes in the straw poll are cast anonymously, diplomatic and other sources close to the Security Council told Middle East Eye that the UK, China and France were the P5 members who had voted to "discourage" Nusseibeh's candidacy.
The US, Russia and Israel - which is not currently part of the Security Council and thus does not vote - all back Nusseibeh, according to the same sources.
In total, the
UAE
minister of state and former ambassador to the UN received seven "encourage" votes, six "discourage" votes and two "no opinion" votes - the same result she achieved in the last straw poll, held on 6 November.
Read more: UK, France and China vote against UAE's Lana Nusseibeh at UN

items.title: Fire at power station in Iraq's Basra kills at least 4, injures 35
items.content:
BASRA, Iraq, Nov 21 (Reuters) - At least 4 people were killed and 35 injured in a fire at a power station in southern Iraq on Saturday, with the toll expected to rise, security officials said.
Civil defence teams brought the fire at the Hartha power station north of Basra under control after firefighters responded to the incident, Iraq's state news agency, INA, reported.
The fire spread to neighbouring houses and forced operations at the power station to stop, the security officials said.

items.title: UK, France and China vote against UAE's Lana Nusseibeh at UN
items.content:
UK, France and China vote against UAE's Lana Nusseibeh at UN
Submitted by
Oscar Rickett
on
Sat, 11/21/2026 - 07:50
Race for secretary-general job remains deadlocked, with Emirati diplomat vowing to continue despite opposition from three P5 countries
UAE's Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh speaks at the United Nations headquarters in New York City, US, 27 October 2026 (David 'Dee' Delgado/Reuters)
Off
Lana Nusseibeh's
bid to become the next secretary-general of the United Nations suffered a setback on Friday after the
UK
,
France
and
China
all voted against the Emirati diplomat in the latest informal straw poll conducted to help determine who should replace Antonio Guterres.
Along with the
US
and
Russia
, the countries make up three of the P5, the permanent members of the UN Security Council that can veto any prospective candidate for the world body's top job.
While votes in the straw poll are cast anonymously, diplomatic and other sources close to the Security Council told Middle East Eye that the UK, China and France were the P5 members who had voted to "discourage" Nusseibeh's candidacy.
The US, Russia and
Israel
- which is not currently part of the Security Council and thus does not vote - all back Nusseibeh, according to the same sources.
In total, the
UAE
minister of state and former ambassador to the UN received seven "encourage" votes, six "discourage" votes and two "no opinion" votes - the same result she achieved in the last straw poll, held on 6 November.
Candidates need to secure at least nine votes to then be put forward to the UN General Assembly, but in order for this to happen they need to have no "discourage" votes.
British MPs urge government to block UAE's Nusseibeh from top UN job
Read More »
The frontrunner, the Costa Rican economist and diplomat Rebeca Grynspan, has 10 encourage votes, but two discourage votes from members of the P5, believed to be Russia and the US.
Argentina's Rafael Grossi, who is backed by his country's far-right president Javier Milei and is favoured - like Nusseibeh - by the US, also picked up three discourage votes from members of the P5.
With no agreement among the P5, the process remains deadlocked.
Nusseibeh has vowed to stay in the race,
posting
on X: "I remain fully committed to this campaign and will continue engaging Member States to earn their support and make the case for a more active, results-focused and responsive United Nations."
Lobbying from the UAE
The results remain a setback for the Abu Dhabi-born diplomat, who has been relentless in her pursuit of the job despite fierce opposition from civil society focused mainly on her country's involvement in the war in
Sudan
.
In her official role in the UAE's government, Nusseibeh has denied reports from the UN Panel of Experts on Abu Dhabi's sponsorship of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force found to have committed genocide in Darfur
by the UN
and the
US
.
On Friday, MEE reported on efforts she had made to lobby Iain Duncan Smith, after the former leader of the UK's Conservative Party
spoke out in parliament
about the UAE's “sponsoring of a huge amount of terrorism in
Sudan
” and called on the British government to use its Security Council veto to block her nomination.
Exclusive: UAE's Nusseibeh lobbied UK's Iain Duncan Smith over UN candidacy
Read More »
The former government minister told MEE that in his meeting with Nusseibeh he reiterated the position he had taken in parliament about the UAE’s involvement in Sudan - denied by Abu Dhabi - and called for the release of “two British citizens wrongly held in Dubai:
Ryan Cornelius and Charles Ridley
”.
Duncan Smith told Nusseibeh that the UAE needed to “cease and desist” from its involvement in the Sudan war.
He told Nusseibeh that her UN candidacy gave the UAE a chance to do the right thing and withdraw from the war in Sudan and release Cornelius and Ridley, two British citizens who have been detained in Dubai for almost 20 years.
“They are corrupt, and they are corrupting,” Duncan Smith said of the Emiratis, before calling on UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to "take a stand".
It would appear that this stand has been taken by Britain, as well as France and China. Nusseibeh and the UAE remain committed to her candidacy, though, and can use what one former British government official described to MEE as "money and investment" as leverage.
Responding to MEE's request for comment on Friday, a spokesperson for Nusseibeh’s campaign said: “Lana Nusseibeh is meeting a wide range of stakeholders as part of her candidacy for UN secretary-general.
"We do not comment on the content of private meetings. Lana has taken a leave of absence from her ministerial role since the submission of her nomination. She took this decision as part of her genuine commitment to the independence of her campaign and potential future role.”

items.title: Pro-Palestine activist Fergie Chambers released, says 'my sacrifice is very small'
items.content:
Pro-Palestine activist Fergie Chambers released, says 'my sacrifice is very small'
Spain's High Court has released pro-Palestinian activist and US media heir Fergie Chambers on conditional bail, while it considers an extradition request by the US, according to a court ruling released on Friday.
The court said it had decided to release Chambers after US authorities acknowledged what they described as substantial and unintentional errors in the Spanish translation of an FBI agent's sworn statement submitted in support of the extradition request.
On his release, Chambers told Reuters he believed the accusations against him were baseless and politically motivated, adding that he had been alone in a cell for what "felt like a long time".
"I'm glad that this is a step in the right direction," he said.
Chambers added: "At the end of the day, I understand that most of the sacrifice I've had to make is very, very small in relation to the struggle that we are all a part of for the Palestinian people, for their liberation, for their sovereignty, for their respect, for the right to live."
"But in the context of just being alone in a cell all the time, it feels like a long time. I just missed my family. I really missed my family and my friends,” Chambers said.
Chambers, whose family owns Cox Enterprises, was arrested at the request of US authorities on 10 July while on holiday in Ibiza. He has been held in custody ever since on accusations including riot, conspiracy to commit riot and international money laundering. Chambers, whose full name is James Cox Chambers Jr, denies wrongdoing.
Separately, Chambers' lawyers said they were challenging a raid by Irish police on his family home in Dublin, which they said was conducted at the request of US authorities and involved the seizure of electronic devices and other property. His legal team said it would seek judicial review unless authorities clarify the legal basis for the operation.
Report by Reuters
Chambers said his sacrifice was very small in relation to the struggle for the Palestinian people (Reuters)

items.title: Morning update
items.content:
Morning update
Good morning, Middle East Eye readers,
If you are just joining us, here are the key developments from across the region and beyond:
* Saudi-led coalition forces say they have intercepted and destroyed several Houthi missiles and drones headed towards Saudi Arabia.
* Six Palestinians were killed and several others injured in Israeli strikes and gunfire across Gaza since Friday.
* Iran still has hope that diplomacy can end its war with the US, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, adding that the two sides are still exchanging messages through mediators.
* A Palestinian man was killed by Israeli forces near Ramallah on Friday as forces carried out raids, detentions and a home demolition across the occupied West Bank. Several Palestinians were also wounded in attacks by settlers and forces in the occupied territory.
* US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to stop it developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping US President Donald Trump’s calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
* Trump has said the International Criminal Court was "out of control", while claiming China "agreed for the first time to condemn the abuses and overreach" of the court, AFP reported.
* Air strikes have targeted Mokha and al-Shamayatayn districts in Taiz governorate of Yemen, Houthi-run Al Masirah TV reports.
* The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said six attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in the past week, while shipping traffic remained about 65 percent below pre-war levels.
* Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its aerospace forces have shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the Strait of Hormuz, state broadcaster Irib reported.
* A senior adviser to the Trump-appointed Gaza Peace Council has warned that the body could return responsibility for the enclave to the United Nations if Israel does not honour its commitments under the 20-point plan, Israeli outlet Ynet has reported.

items.title: Fire at Iraqi power station leaves four dead, 30 injured
items.content:
Fire at Iraqi power station leaves four dead, 30 injured
At least four people were killed and 30 injured in a fire at a power station in southern Iraq on Saturday, with the toll expected to rise, security officials said.
Civil defence teams brought the fire at the Hartha power station north of Basra under control after firefighters responded to the incident, Iraq's state news agency, INA, reported.
The fire spread to neighbouring houses and forced operations at the power station to stop, the security officials said.
The Hartha station has an installed generating capacity of 800 megawatts but had been operating at around 400 megawatts before the fire, they said.
There was no immediate official information on the cause of the fire or the extent of the damage, INA reported.
Report by Reuters

items.title: Seven Gazans wounded, one critically, in Israeli gunfire and air strikes
items.content:
Seven Gazans wounded, one critically, in Israeli gunfire and air strikes
Seven Palestinians were injured, one of them critically, in Israeli gunfire and air strikes across Gaza on Saturday morning, Wafa reported.
Two Palestinians were shot by Israeli forces in displacement camps in the town of Jabalia, north of the Strip, while a woman and a child were wounded after tanks opened heavy fire towards tents for displaced people in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, Wafa said.
Meanwhile, three Palestinians were injured, one of them critically, in an Israeli air strike targeting an area south of Al-Mawasi.
According to Gaza health authorities, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed and over 6,000 wounded since the ceasefire began in October last year.

items.title: Rights group calls for ban on white phosphorus, cites Israel's use in Gaza
items.content:
Rights group calls for ban on white phosphorus, cites Israel's use in Gaza
Cairo-based rights group, Maat for Peace, Development and Human Rights, has called for an explicit ban on the use of white phosphorus, which has repeatedly been used by Israel in Gaza and southern Lebanon, Al Jazeera reported.
White phosphorus can cause severe burns, ignite repeatedly and produce intense heat and toxic smoke.
Human rights groups and The New York Times said in June that they had documented Israel's use of the chemical white phosphorus over civilian areas in Lebanon.
White phosphorus is not banned under international law, but it is illegal to use the chemical in and near populated areas since it can cause widespread harm. Israel has been accused by the international human rights community for decades of using the substance in a way that puts civilians in danger.
In a working paper submitted at the review session for the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, the group said the current treaty has glaring gaps that allow for the use of white phosphorus.
Following an impasse after talks started on Monday, the conference ran over time and ended early on Saturday, with states agreeing to continue talks aimed at developing measures on lethal autonomous weapons by 2028.

items.title: 'Cycle of conflicts must end': Leaders and experts call for cooperation on Middle East conflicts
items.content:
'Cycle of conflicts must end': Leaders and experts call for cooperation on Middle East conflicts
Regional and international leaders and experts called for dialogue and cooperation to promote stability in the Middle East at the 12th edition of the MED - Mediterranean Dialogues, held in Naples from 19-21 November.
Promoted by Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation and the Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI), the conference brought together regional and international leaders to discuss Middle East conflicts, security cooperation, maritime threats and prospects for regional stability.
MED Dialogues shared on X
key remarks by speakers on Middle East-related issues.
"Dialogue is essential. The security of any country depends on the stability of its neighbourhood, including Iran. We need to create space for mutual security guarantees - not to end one conflict only for another cycle to begin, but to build an interdependent security arrangement that respects the interests of all."
Manal Radwan, adviser and special envoy to the Saudi foreign minister for negotiations and peace efforts, Saudi Arabia
"The Mecca Agreement is not an alternative to Turkey’s existing alliances, but a complementary one. Turkey joined it to reinforce deterrence and build upon the capabilities of the three countries involved. It does not name anyone in the region as an enemy and allows other regional powers to be part of it."
Çağrı Erhan, chief adviser to the Turkish president
"Geography shapes maritime security challenges, but addressing them is a shared responsibility. Securing the Red Sea and the Arabian Gulf is not only the responsibility of the countries along their shores: it requires the entire international community, because trade through these routes serves the whole world."
Walid al-Khuraiji, Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs
"We need to be at the table whenever Yemen’s future is discussed. Decisions about our country cannot be made without our presence."
Afrah al-Zouba, Yemen's minister of foreign affairs and expatriates
"The Palestinian position is clear: the world must remain focused on international law. Today, it is under serious threat and subject to the hegemony of a few countries. The international community must reclaim it, and the UN has a crucial role to play.”
Varsen Aghabekian Shahin, Palestinian minister of foreign affairs and expatriates
"Gulf states will continue to deepen their relationship with the United States while diversifying globally. We cannot afford to stand by, watch this unfold and close our borders. What we should be doing - and what we are doing right now - is coming together and maximising our capabilities through cooperation.”
Majed al-Ansari, adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign ministry spokesperson
"The Strait of Hormuz gives Iran leverage rooted in geography, and that leverage cannot be bombed away. We need a formula in which Iran feels secure and regional countries feel their rights are respected. The solution must pass through the region."
Ali Vaez, deputy director, Middle East programme, International Crisis Group
"The future of Iran is an Iranian issue that requires Iranian agency. Iranians are not looking to the US or Israel to determine it, but we still do not know what that agency will look like or when it will materialise. War has only bought the system some time."
Sanam Vakil, director, Middle East and North Africa programme, Chatham House
"There is a lesson here for everyone: the problems in the Red Sea are caused by human beings fighting against each other, not by natural forces. People need to sit down and talk, because the price is paid not only by Egypt, but by everyone. What will make the difference is how the world collaborates to solve the problems.
Abla Abdel Latif, executive director and director of research, Egyptian Center for Economic Studies
"People in Lebanon are tired of being told to be resilient. We need to move beyond acting solely as implementers and be ready to hand over to local communities - but without transferring risk to them. Humanitarian action must be linked to recovery and development.”
Imran Riza, UN deputy special coordinator for Lebanon
"Inclusion means that all Syrians feel this process belongs to them and that they can feel at home in the new Syria. Justice must apply to every perpetrator, regardless of who they are or who their victims are - there can be no selective justice. Institutional development takes time, and the clock is ticking."
Claudio Cordone, UN deputy special envoy for Syria
"Syria needs stability before it can benefit from its position. Beyond corridors and trade routes, what matters most is the lives of the Syrian people. That must be the priority - especially when three million people are still looking for a home.”
Samir Aita, president, the Circle of Arab Economists
"We should not see Lebanon’s mosaic society as inherently fragile or vulnerable, but as rich and complex. Its religious and ethnic communities are not a weakness: they are the building blocks of a strong country for the future."
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, secretary for relations with states and international organisations, Holy See

items.title: Gaza Board of Peace says it will hand keys to UN if Israel fails to honour commitments
items.content:
Gaza Board of Peace says it will hand keys to UN if Israel fails to honour commitments
A senior adviser to the Donald Trump-appointed Gaza Peace Council has warned that the body could return responsibility for the enclave to the United Nations if Israel does not honour its commitments under the 20-point plan, Israeli outlet Ynet has reported.
Josh Gruenbaum, who was appointed to the council by Trump and previously worked in the White House, told Ynet: “We have been extremely patient and have given Israel its space. But it is frustrating that now, with the elections behind us - even if they haven’t resulted in a clear coalition - that Israel is failing to move forward on the commitments [Benjamin] Netanyahu made to President Trump.”
“If this political leadership says it no longer wants to honour what they committed to, just let us know,” Gruenbaum said, “and we will throw the keys back to the UN.”
Ynet said it had seen a presentation prepared by council members, who visited Israel last week. Its final slide, titled “Other alternatives to Gaza”, reportedly lists several scenarios if the plan is abandoned.
These include a future US administration and Congress ordering a different reconstruction plan, the UN Security Council taking over “perhaps through UNRWA”, the Palestinian Authority and Hamas.
The last scenario, according to the slide, is that Israel becomes fully responsible for the administrative and humanitarian costs of Gaza’s population.
Another slide reportedly says Hamas formally accepted the plan in July, pledging to give up its weapons and transfer governmental powers to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), the technocratic body meant to run the territory.
“We are at a standstill due to political elements within the Netanyahu government who have prevented us from progressing and from testing whether Hamas will keep its word,” Gruenbaum said, according to Ynet.
Gruenbaum also criticises Israel for failing to allow sufficient aid into Gaza before winter sets in (AFP)

items.content:
Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet
Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.
Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

items.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
items.content:
Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access
When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.
He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars.
The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.

items.title: Israel has not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers, Ocha says
items.content:
Israel has not acted on calls to protect Palestinian olive farmers, Ocha says
Calls on the Israeli authorities to protect Palestinian olive farmers and ensure they can reach their groves safely have not been acted upon, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said, citing the Humanitarian Country Team.
Instead, in the first nine months of 2026, Israeli authorities uprooted or otherwise damaged more than 10,000 Palestinian-owned trees and saplings across the West Bank, mostly olives, the statement adds.
The Humanitarian Country Team for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which brings together UN bodies and humanitarian NGOs, said more than 400 Israeli settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest since September have resulted in casualties or damage to property, including to more than 4,000 trees and saplings.
The number of attacks this year exceeds that recorded in any previous olive harvest season. This year’s harvesting window is closing, the team said, but there is still some time to act.
"Humanitarian NGOs and UN agencies urge the Israeli authorities in the strongest possible terms: end all attacks on Palestinians and their livelihoods, as required by international law. Ensure farmers have free, safe, sufficient and reliable access to their land. The team added that perpetrators must be stopped and held to account," the statement read.

items.title: UNDP official: 'Gaza's suffering must compel us to ask difficult questions'
items.content:
UNDP official: 'Gaza's suffering must compel us to ask difficult questions'
A top United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) official has said the suffering endured by people in Gaza "must compel us to ask difficult questions".
“What strikes you immediately is the scale of the destruction in Gaza, where more than 90% of the population depends on humanitarian assistance. The contrast between what we consider normal—food, water and quality of life—and the suffering endured by people in Gaza must compel us to ask difficult questions,” Haoliang Xu, Under-Secretary-General and Associate Administrator, UNDP, said.
Xu said a defining feature of our time is "polycrisis, with challenges that extend far beyond any one place", according to a post on X by MED Dialogues.
"The conflict in the Middle East, for example, is costing countries across the region at least 3.6% of GDP, with some UNDP estimates reaching 6%,” Xu said.

items.title: Several Palestinians injured in attacks by Israeli settlers, forces in West Bank
items.content:
Several Palestinians injured in attacks by Israeli settlers, forces in West Bank
Several Palestinians were injured in a wave of attacks by Israeli settlers and military across the occupied West Bank, according to reports by the Palestinian news agency, Wafa, and Al Jazeera.
* The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its crew treated a Palestinian man who was beaten by Israeli forces in the town of Jaba', south of Jenin.
*Israeli soldiers opened fire at a vehicle in the Qabatiya town, south of Jenin, and detained two inhabitants.
* Ahmed Kawazbeh, head of Al-Maniya village council, southeast of Bethlehem, tells Wafa that a group of Israeli settlers raided the home of Mohammad Khalil Jabareen early Thursday morning and attacked his family members with batons and pepper spray. Jabareen's son, Raafat, and his wife sustained bruises and injuries and suffered from suffocation while attempting to protect their children. They were taken to Beit Jala Governmental Hospital for treatment.
The attackers also smashed the family’s vehicle. Kawazbeh said this was the second time the family had been targeted in a settler attack.
*Israeli forces arrested at least 17 Palestinians, including former prisoners, in raids across the occupied West Bank. About 20 others were detained in Tubas and Tammun, where soldiers turned a house into a military post, according to Al Jazeera.
*Israeli settlers shot and wounded a Palestinian olive picker in Nabi Saleh, northwest of Ramallah, and assaulted others harvesting olives in Berin, east of Hebron.
*Israeli forces demolished a Palestinian home in al-Mazraa al-Gharbiya, northwest of Ramallah, and prevented residents of Khirbet Samra in the northern Jordan Valley from repairing tents damaged by heavy rain, according to Al Jazeera.
*Footage released by Israeli rights group, Mistaclim, shows a group of Israeli settlers stealing fruit and vegetables from a roadside vendor during an incursion into the village of Al Fundukumiya, in Jenin.

items.title: UKMTO weekly report says six vessels attacked in and around Hormuz
items.content:
UKMTO weekly report says six vessels attacked in and around Hormuz
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) has said six attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz were reported in the past week, while shipping traffic remained about 65 percent below pre-war levels.
In its weekly report published on Friday, UKMTO said four of the six incidents occurred in the Strait of Hormuz and two in the Arabian Gulf.
The UKMTO recorded 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits during the seven days to November 18, including US-facilitated movements. The combined figure was down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound the previous week.
Around half of Strait of Hormuz transits involved energy carriers. Most vessels broadcasting AIS continued to use the Iranian route, although UKMTO noted an increase in traffic along the southern route.
No attacks were recorded in the past week in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandab, with the last confirmed attack recorded on August 24. However, vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb remain about 22 percent below levels existing before 22 July when Houthis announced a blockade.

Trump: 'ICC out of control, can't go in and arrest heads of countries'
US President Donald Trump has said the International Criminal Court was "out of control", while claiming China "agreed for the first time to condemn the abuses and overreach" of the court, AFP reported.
Trump, on his return from a summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, complained that the ICC believes "they can go in and arrest the heads of countries, and they can't do that. They can do it for no reason -- so we condemned that as a group."
Washington has vowed to dismantle the court, which it targeted with new sanctions last month. Trump has been angered by the tribunal's move to issue an arrest warrant for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over Gaza genocide.

items.title: Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza, civil defence says
items.content:
Six Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza, civil defence says
Israeli strikes killed six people in the Gaza Strip on Friday, the civil defence agency in the war-shattered territory told AFP, despite a ceasefire.
Mahmoud Bassal, the spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, said that four Palestinians were killed and several others wounded in an Israeli airstrike southwest of Bureij refugee camp in the central Gaza Strip on Friday.
The civil defence also said one Palestinian was killed in an Israeli drone strike targeting a tent in the Al-Munasara camp for displaced people in Deir al-Balah.
Another person was killed in a drone strike north of Nuseirat refugee camp, also in the central Gaza Strip.
The Israeli military told AFP it had "targeted multiple military operatives" in several strikes, which came a day after the army said it had completed a ground incursion in the central Gaza Strip.
More than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the ceasefire, according to an AFP tally based on data from the Gaza health ministry whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Report by AFP

items.title: Loud explosion heard in Riyadh after Saudi civil defence alerts
items.content:
Loud explosion heard in Riyadh after Saudi civil defence alerts
A loud boom was heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh late hours on Friday, a witness told Reuters, shortly after the kingdom’s civil defence issued an alert warning of potential danger in the city.
The civil defence sent a second message soon afterwards saying the danger had passed. The cause of the boom was not immediately clear.
It was the first such alert in Riyadh since a Houthi attack struck the capital’s tallest skyscraper on Thursday.
Earlier, the civil defence issued a similar alert for al-Sulayyil governorate, in central Saudi Arabia, before later saying the danger there had also passed.

items.title: Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
items.content:
Vance refuses to endorse Iran strikes despite pressure from Trump
US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to stop it developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping Trump’s calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February had been the president’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States”.
After the midterm elections, Vance blamed the war for the Republicans’ historic losses and called for the US to exit the conflict.
His statement, posted on social media, was widely seen as a break with Trump as the vice president weighs a 2028 White House bid.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance
wrote
. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.”
Trump said on Friday that he was not unhappy with Vance’s conclusion but that it lacked a crucial element: an acknowledgement that the strikes were necessary and that Vance would make the same decision.
“People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion,” Trump said. “But I say, I know the Iranians, and, frankly, they’re crazy.”
Vice President JD Vance on Iran: "The goal of keeping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon is absolutely what we need to be doing. It's the biggest state sponsored terrorism. If they had a nuclear weapon, they would use it as leverage or God forbid they would attack and kill thousands, hundreds of thousands potentially, of innocent people. The president is the one who makes the decision and the president has said he would do it again. And my view is that my goal is and my job is to support the President of the United States."
— Vice President JD Vance (@VP)
November 20, 2026

items.title: Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
items.content:
Iran wants Trump to state explicitly he wants a deal, Araghchi says
Iran still has hope that diplomacy can end its war with the United States, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said, adding that the two sides are still exchanging messages through mediators.
“We are seeking an agreement with the US that would ensure there is no further war afterwards,” Araghchi told an Iranian newspaper.
He said Tehran saw no need to change the intermediaries in the talks.
Before going any further, Iran wants guarantees that Washington is serious about negotiating, he said, and it has discussed the form and nature of possible confidence-building measures with the mediators.
Iran’s first demand is for US President Donald Trump to state explicitly that he wants an agreement, Araghchi said.
He added that it was not surprising for Trump to take a new position every day, or even to reverse what he had said the day before.
One of Iran’s red lines is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country, Araghchi stated, though he believed a fair solution could be reached.
He also said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the US met Iran’s seven conditions.
His comments came hours after Trump reiterated that the US had "total control" over the strait.
Iran’s official position on the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons remains the same, and its nuclear doctrine has not changed, Araghchi added.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi speaks during a meeting with foreign ambassadors, in Tehran, Iran, on 16 June 2026 (Iranian Foreign Ministry/WANA)

items.title: Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran
items.content:
Inside the Iraqi Kurdish city caught between the US and Iran
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Fri, 11/20/2026 - 19:37
Sulaymaniyah is reeling from the economic toll of the Iran war and grappling with an emboldened regional power next door
A market in the city of Sulaymaniyah in Iraq's Kurdistan Region is said to be the largest bazaar in the region, on 11 November 2026 (Sean Mathews/MEE)
Off
If
US
President Donald Trump has his way, Baran* will be out of business.
The thirty-year-old Kurd is a trader who buys diesel in Iraq and sells it in Afghanistan. It’s a stressful gig, but one that can generate a tidy profit in a place like Iraqi Kurdistan. A truck laden with $20,000 worth of diesel in Iraq can sell in Kabul for around $24,000, leaving around $2,000 for the trader once expenses are paid. But it has to make it through
Iran
first.
“The journey is more dangerous now. It’s harder to find drivers. The border isn’t as reliable. The price of diesel has also shot up,” Baran, whose name has been changed to protect his identity, told Middle East Eye.
Trump says instead of restarting strikes on Iran, he wants to choke its economy. In addition to a naval blockade, the US is pressing countries like
Turkey
,
Iraq
and
Pakistan
to seal their borders with Iran. Earlier this month, the US announced a task force to blockade trade across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Baran has no political beef with the US. On the contrary, he says, “George W. Bush overthrew Saddam Hussein. He helped Kurdistan. I don’t prefer Iran to the US,” he said over a glass of anise-flavoured Arak and hookahs at a restaurant in Sulaymaniyah.
“But this war has not been good for business or our economy.”
Baran is a microcosm of the city he calls home.
Sulaymaniyah
Nestled in the Zagros Mountains, Sulaymaniyah is Iraqi Kurdistan’s second largest city. Its beating heart is a sprawling bazaar where locals boast that any item a shopper desires can be procured. November is pomegranate season, and the fruit was plentiful. The label “Made In Iran” on packages and wrappings was also ubiquitous.
Sulaymaniyah prides itself on being more libertine than its rival Erbil. In the bazaar, more women go without a headscarf than with one.
“If people have $50 in their pockets, they will spend it to go out here,” Baran said. Bazaar merchants flick the city’s famed prayer beads, made of pistachio tree seeds, and tea boys run around keeping everyone well caffeinated.
On the surface, the vibrant bazaar gives an impression of prosperity, but the opposite is true.
“The price of food is unbearable for most people now. For some products, the increase is 200 percent,” Evin*, a 28-year-old shopper, complained to MEE. “We used to import so much from Iran, but now they aren’t exporting.”
Another young professional said they had to delay purchasing a new laptop computer because the price had shot up from $600 to $800 since the war started.
Because of taxes and logistics, Sulaymaniyah’s most competitive trade corridor to China runs through Iran. The region has a plethora of border posts that are more convenient than the Iraqi port of Basra - which feels a world away from here - or Turkey. Goods coming from the latter are also subject to higher taxes from Turkey and Erbil.
“In Iraqi Kurdistan, trade with Iran is a major part of the local economy,” Dlawer Ala’Aldeen, the president of the Middle East Research Institute, a Kurdish think-tank in Erbil, told MEE.
The US-Israeli war on Iran is taking a toll across the region. The economies of all the Arabian Gulf states are expected to shrink this year. Their pitches as tourism and business hubs are in jeopardy. This month alone, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund headquarters and the tower housing state-oil company Aramco in Riyadh came under attack from the Houthis.
But Iraqi Kurdistan is a unique case.
'Living on a thin margin'
The region is convulsed by an internal political fissure that experts say could increase the sway of outside powers, particularly Turkey and Iran. This semiautonomous region of Iraq also lacks the deep pockets of Arab Gulf states to cushion geopolitical blows. The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) has been plagued by financial difficulties for years.
The region is supposed to receive around 15 percent of Iraq’s federal budget, more than 90 percent of which comes from oil revenue. Despite the war on Iran, Iraq exported more oil this month than at any time since 2019, but payments to the KRG are late.
Government employees are receiving their salaries months behind schedule. The rising costs of the Iran war have only compounded the pain.
Vehicles drive at the Iraq-Iran border crossing of Bashmagh near Sulaimaniyah in Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, on 11 March 2026 (AFP)
Iran has deep trade ties across Iraq and the Kurdistan Region. But Sulaymaniyah is particularly close to its eastern neighbour. The city was founded in 1784 under the Baban Emirate, which controlled parts of modern-day Iraq and Iran. Many founding Kurdish families hail from across the border.
“Slemani was already living on a thin margin,” Ala’Aldeen said, adding that the local economy depends on “cross-border trade, business, daily labour, and goods” from Iran.
“The war did not create that fragility; it exposed it: when Hormuz closed and when the United States pressed Iraq to close all but two crossings with Iran, Slemani felt it in prices and availability of goods,” he said. “Cutting Iran off will leave Slemani without many alternatives.”
Those trade ties are more interesting when one considers the pressure Iraq’s Kurdistan Region came under to join in the US-Israeli war on Iran earlier this year.
An estimated 40 million Kurds live between Syria, Iraq, Turkey and Iran. Although they never got a country when the Middle East was carved up by European colonial powers, Iraqi Kurdistan gained a high degree of autonomy in the 21st century because of the support it received from the US after the US invasion of Iraq.
For more than 20 years, Peshmerga fighters have been key American allies, most recently against the Islamic State militant group. The KRG also hosts some Iranian-Kurdish opposition groups who are backed by the US and Israel. When the Trump administration and Israel decided to attack Iran, they turned to Iraq’s Kurds to support opposition groups and fight across the border, but that plan never fully materialised.
'Impossible position to be in'
The KRG is dominated by two family dynasties, the Barzani family in Erbil, which leads the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), and the Talabani family in Sulaymaniyah, which leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
In the 1990s, Iraq’s Kurds fought a civil war which saw the PUK receive support from Iran, and the KDP from Turkey. Because of its geography and economy, Sulaymaniyah continues to be viewed as closer to Iran, so much so that Bafel Talabani, the PUK leader, denied a reporter's question at a conference earlier this month in Sulaymaniyah, put to him that he was in Iran’s “pocket”.
In reality, both the PUK and KDP are closely aligned with the US.
Female members of the Iranian Kurdish opposition Komala party carry the body of a Peshmerga fighter in the autonomous Kurdistan region, on 16 April 2026 (AFP)
Among American officials,
Bafel Talabani
is known to enjoy hanging out with former American Joint Special Operations Command fighters, better known as “JSOC guys”. His brother, Qubad, the deputy prime minister of Iraqi Kurdistan, is married to a former State Department official.
A former US intelligence official told MEE that the PUK was actually seen by members of the Trump administration as more receptive to plans to support Kurdish opposition groups in Iran because it was lobbying for greater attention in Washington. The PUK's territory in the KRG also shares a longer border with Iran.
The PUK was courting the Trump administration in part over frustration that its rival, the KDP, had greater access in Washington as a result of controlling the Kurdistan region’s presidency.
The tensions between the two parties have erupted into a major political rift that experts say risks splitting the KRG. Talabani withdrew the PUK from the region's parliament in November and told a forum in Sulaymaniyah that the KRG was already living “the reality of two governments and two administrations”.
In the end, neither the PUK nor KDP joined the US war effort. A decision that many Kurds welcomed.
"Kurdistan was right to refuse to be embroiled in this war. A collapse in Tehran would not arrive as a clean handover. It would arrive as chaos on Kurdistan's longest border: refugees, armed factions, a power vacuum, and a fight over who controls Iranian Kurdistan," Ala’Aldeen at the  Middle East Research Institute, told MEE.
Internal politics are at play now, too.
Bafel Talabani is courting members of Baghdad’s ruling Shia Coordination Framework for an upper hand against the KDP. The Shia Coordination Framework is aligned with Tehran.
The Kurdistan Region is also militarily exposed. It lacks proper air defence systems. The last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq. The region faced hundreds of Iranian missile and drone strikes
during the war.
“Bafel Talabani is an ambitious guy. He speaks with everyone, too. He’s pragmatic. But he faces a very difficult position. He is seeking US support, but Iran sees Sulaymaniyah as its backyard. It’s an impossible position to be in,” Oral Toga, a senior researcher at the Centre for Iranian Studies in Ankara, told MEE.
'Iran has the upper hand'
At a strategic forum hosted in Sulaymaniyah earlier this month, PUK officials emphasised their desire for dialogue and partnership with Iran. Bafel Talabani himself
said
that Iran had emerged “stronger but different” from the US-Israeli war and criticised those who characterise the country as being run by “mad mullahs”.
Recounting a recent trip he made to Iran, he offered a very different assessment to that proposed by members of the Trump administration who have characterised Iran as on the verge of economic collapse.
"I thought I was in London," Talabani said, noting that "less than 50 percent of ladies and girls had scarves" and that restaurants were filled with young people dancing.
This overview shows Iraq's northeastern city of Sulaymaniyah in the autonomous Kurdistan region at sunset, on 18 October 2024 (AFP)
Tehran is now pressuring Iraqi Kurdistan to clamp down on Kurdish opposition groups. In a meeting in September with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Bafal Talabani promised not to allow Iraqi Kurdistan to become "a haven for harming or threatening" the Islamic Republic.
"As an ally of Mr Trump and, strangely, an ally of the Iranians [I say] the mighty US can [talk to Iran],” he said at the forum.
“The region feels Iran has a strategic upper hand at the moment. It’s not just Iraqi Kurdistan, but the Gulf states too. They all want to avoid Iran’s wrath," Sarhang Hamasaeed, an independent Middle East analyst, told MEE.
“But Iran has shown that in this fight it isn’t factoring those relations in. Iraq has been the economic lungs of Iran, but Iran didn’t spare their exports through Hormuz," he added.
Given its land border with Iran, Sulaymaniyah is even more vulnerable to reprisals should the war resume.
"The Kurds in Iraq were Iran's target practice in prior years, well before Iran's war with the US and Israel. They know, and don't want to be on the receiving end of Iranian strikes," Hamasaeed said.
“Between the US and Iran, they have to appease Iran more, because Trump won’t strike them with drones and missiles  - Iran will,” he said.
The US will not fire missiles at Iraqi Kurdistan like Iran, but America's foreign policy could endanger the region.
Many in Sulaymaniyah believe the US will not be content until it collapses the Iranian government.
Trump himself said as much on a radio show this month. When asked by a radio host whether he would consider it a “defeat” for him if the Islamic Republic was still in power at the end of his term, Trump said “absolutely”.
"The worst thing for Sulaymaniyah and Iraqi Kurdistan would be a failed state across the border. We need stability," a Kurdish official in the city told MEE.

items.title: US sanctions Iranian 'oil trustees' it accuses of evading sanctions
items.content:
US sanctions Iranian 'oil trustees' it accuses of evading sanctions
The US Treasury on Friday imposed sanctions on four Iranians who served as "oil trustees".
It said they had sought to collect funds from illicit international oil sales and pass them to the Iranian government to evade earlier sanctions and a US naval blockade.
In many cases, the trustees kept the oil revenues for personal gain, the Treasury said in a statement.
Those sanctioned include Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former intelligence officer in Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and Majid Taj, brother of Mehdi Taj, the president of Iran’s football federation.

items.title: Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
items.content:
Palestinian man killed near Ramallah as Israeli raids sweep occupied West Bank
A Palestinian man was killed by Israeli forces near Ramallah on Friday as the forces carried out raids, detentions and a home demolition across the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Hamza Masoud Salim Abdo, 42, was killed in Dura al-Qare, northeast of Ramallah, by Israeli forces who are still withholding his body, the Palestinian General Authority of Civil Affairs said.
In Jaba, south of Jenin, Israeli forces beat a man who was taken to hospital, the Palestinian Red Crescent said. A convoy of army vehicles later stormed the town and detained two young men. In nearby Qabatiya, soldiers fired on a vehicle and detained two people.
In Jericho, a young Palestinian man was shot in the foot during a raid on the al-Bayader neighbourhood.
South of Hebron, Israeli forces raided al-Fawwar refugee camp as residents left Friday prayers, firing tear gas and beating a young man who was later hospitalised.
In nearby Beit Ummar, Israeli forces stormed the town, ordered merchants to close their shops and fired barrages of tear gas and stun grenades, according to local media activist Mohammad Awad. He said soldiers severely beat and detained two men, aged 22 and 45.
In the Tulkarm governorate, several young men were detained as Israeli forces raided the town of Anabta.
Also on Friday, Israeli bulldozers demolished a home in al-Mazra’a al-Gharbiya, northwest of Ramallah.
Meanwhile, Israeli settlers stole the contents of a roadside fruit stand south of Jenin and trees from a nursery in Jaba, surveillance footage showed.
Israeli soldiers block a road, preventing access to Palestinian-owned olive groves during harvest season, in Abu Falah near Ramallah, occupied West Bank, on 20 November 2026 (Reuters/Ammar Awad)

items.title: US Vice President Vance declines to say he would have ordered Iran strikes
items.content:
By Bo Erickson and Jacob Bogage
WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US Vice President JD Vance on Friday declined to say whether he would have authorized strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon, sidestepping President Donald Trump's calls for him to say the attacks were necessary and that he would carry them out again.
Speaking at a White House press conference alongside Trump, Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February was Trump's call, "and my job is to support the president of the United States."
